events.title: Rise of Nubian Civilization
events.description: Early Nubian civilization emerged in northern Sudan's Nile Valley, known for pottery making and pastoralism. Nubians developed unique culture while maintaining trade relations with Egypt. Archaeological evidence shows complex social structures and religious beliefs during this period. Nubia's rich gold resources made it important trading center in ancient world.

events.title: Kingdom of Kush Established
events.description: Nubians established Kingdom of Kush in northern Sudan with capital at Kerma. Kush controlled vast territory between Second and Sixth Cataracts of Nile, becoming one of ancient Africa's most powerful kingdoms. Kingdom renowned for gold mining, ivory trade and sophisticated bronze craftsmanship.

events.title: Kerma Culture Flourishes
events.description: Kerma became political and economic center of Kush Kingdom, developing unique Kerma culture. City featured large fortifications, palaces and temples. Kerma pottery, famous for its fine black-topped red ware, became hallmark of Nubian civilization. Kingdom maintained frequent trade with Egypt while preserving political independence.

events.title: Egyptian New Kingdom Conquest
events.description: Egyptian Pharaoh Thutmose I conquered Nubia, making Kush Egyptian colony. Egypt established viceroyalty in Nubia, extensively mining gold resources. During this period Nubia heavily influenced by Egyptian culture, adopting Egyptian religion, art and architecture. Many Nubian nobles sent to Egypt for education.

events.title: Kush Kingdom Revival
events.description: With Egyptian New Kingdom's decline, Kush regained independence and moved capital to Napata. Kushite kings adopted Egyptian pharaonic titles and ceremonies while maintaining Nubian traditions. Kingdom regained control of Nubian gold mines and trade routes, gradually restoring power.

events.title: Napatan Kingdom Consolidation
events.description: Kush Kingdom established strong political and religious center at Napata. Temple of Amun became kingdom's spiritual pillar, with priestly class wielding enormous influence. Kingdom developed unique Nubian-Egyptian hybrid culture, building pyramid tombs smaller and steeper than Egyptian pyramids. This period laid foundation for later conquest of Egypt.

events.title: Kushite Conquest of Egypt
events.description: Kushite King Piye conquered Egypt, establishing Twenty-fifth Dynasty, known as 'Black Pharaohs' era. Kushite rulers governed Egypt for nearly century, promoting Egyptian cultural renaissance, restoring ancient temples and traditional religious ceremonies. This was glorious period in African history, with Kush becoming major Mediterranean power.

events.title: Assyrian Invasion
events.description: Assyrian Empire invaded Egypt, forcing Kushite rulers to withdraw to Nubia. Despite losing control of Egypt, Kush continued prospering in Sudan region. Kingdom strengthened Red Sea trade connections, developed iron manufacturing technology, and culture and arts reached new heights.

events.title: Pharaoh Psamtik II's Invasion
events.description: Egyptian Twenty-sixth Dynasty Pharaoh Psamtik II led army deep into Nubia, destroying Kushite military installations and temple inscriptions. Though this expedition did not conquer Kush, it severely damaged kingdom's prestige. Kushite rulers forced to strengthen southern defenses, prompting later capital relocation further south to Meroë. This conflict accelerated end of Napatan period.

events.title: Capital Moved to Meroë
events.description: Kingdom of Kush moved capital from Napata to Meroë, marking beginning of Meroitic period. Meroë's location was more secure, distant from northern threats. During this period Kush developed unique Meroitic script, built numerous pyramids, and became iron manufacturing center. Kingdom maintained extensive trade relations with Rome, India and Arabia.

events.title: Roman-Meroitic War
events.description: After Egypt became Roman province, Kingdom of Meroë clashed with Rome. Kandake (Queen) Amanirenas led Meroitic forces to raid southern Egypt. Roman forces counterattacked and briefly occupied Napata. Eventually both sides reached peace agreement, establishing border between two nations. This conflict demonstrated Meroitic Kingdom's military strength.

events.title: Meroitic Civilization at Its Peak
events.description: Kingdom of Meroë reached its zenith, becoming one of strongest states in sub-Saharan Africa. Kingdom built hundreds of pyramids, developed sophisticated iron-smelting technology, exported iron goods throughout Africa. Meroitic script widely used in royal inscriptions and religious texts. Kingdom controlled important trade routes connecting Mediterranean, Red Sea and African interior.

events.title: Meroitic Decline
events.description: Kingdom of Meroë began declining, possibly due to environmental degradation from overgrazing, shifting trade routes, and pressure from Noba people from south and Aksum from east. Quality of royal pyramid construction declined, inscriptions decreased. Central authority weakened, local powers rose. This created conditions for eventual Aksumite conquest.

events.title: Aksumite Conquest of Meroë
events.description: Ethiopian Kingdom of Aksum conquered Meroë, ending Kingdom of Kush. This marked end of Nubian classical civilization. Aksumite conquest brought Christianity's spread, changing religious and cultural landscape of northern Sudan. Many Nubians began converting to Christianity.

events.title: Noba Migration
events.description: Noba people migrated from western desert into Nile Valley, filling power vacuum after Meroë Kingdom's collapse. Noba mixed with local Nubians, forming new social structures. This period witnessed transition from classical Meroitic civilization to medieval Nubian kingdoms. Tribal confederations gradually evolved into organized kingdoms.

events.title: Nubian Conversion to Christianity
events.description: Byzantine Empire sent missionary Julian to Nubia, and Nobatian king converted to Christianity. This marked beginning of large-scale Christianization of Nubia. Coptic Church became main religious form, with Greek and Coptic languages used in religious ceremonies. Nubian Church developed unique liturgical practices and artistic styles, blending local traditions with Byzantine influences.

events.title: Nubian Christian Kingdoms
events.description: Three Christian kingdoms established in northern Sudan: Nobatia, Makuria and Alodia. These kingdoms adopted Coptic Christianity, building numerous churches and monasteries. Nubian Christian art combined Byzantine, Coptic and local traditional elements, forming unique style. Kingdoms maintained close relations with Byzantine Empire and Egypt.

events.title: Arab Conquest of Egypt
events.description: After Arab Muslims conquered Egypt, they began expanding south into Nubia. Nubian Christian kingdoms signed Baqt Treaty with Arabs, agreeing to provide annual tribute of slaves and gold in exchange for peaceful coexistence. This treaty lasted several centuries and was important document in medieval diplomatic history.

events.title: Makuria Kingdom Unification
events.description: Kingdom of Makuria annexed Nobatia, becoming most powerful Christian kingdom in northern Sudan with capital at Dongola. Kingdom maintained complex diplomatic relations with Islamic Egypt, involving both trade and military conflicts. Makurian church architecture and mural art reached peak, displaying unique Nubian Christian culture.

events.title: Nubian Christian Golden Age
events.description: Kingdom of Makuria entered golden age, with magnificent structures like Faras Cathedral rising. Nubian mural art reached pinnacle, with vibrant colors and exquisite techniques. Kingdom controlled Nile trade, enjoying economic prosperity. Nubian and Greek languages used in written records. During this period Nubian culture developed independently from Egypt and Byzantium, forming unique African Christian civilization.

events.title: Mamluk Invasion of Makuria
events.description: Egyptian Mamluk Sultan sent army to invade Makuria, capturing capital Dongola. Though kingdom survived, it was forced to become Egyptian vassal, paying annual tribute. Muslim merchants and tribes began migrating to Nubia in large numbers, with Islamic influence gradually expanding. This invasion marked beginning of decline of Nubian Christian kingdoms.

events.title: Fall of Makuria Kingdom
events.description: Last Nubian Christian kingdom Makuria conquered by Muslims, marking end of Nubian Christian era. Islam began spreading widely in northern Sudan, with Arab culture gradually replacing Nubian traditions. Many Christian churches converted to mosques.

events.title: Arab Tribal Migration
events.description: Large numbers of Arab Bedouin tribes migrated from Egypt into Sudan, bringing Islam and Arabic language. These tribes intermarried with local Nubians, forming new hybrid society. Arabization and Islamization processes accelerated, with Nubian language gradually replaced by Arabic. Nomadic and agricultural economies coexisted, forming Sudan's unique social structure.

events.title: Funj Sultanate Established
events.description: Funj people established Funj Sultanate at confluence of Blue and White Niles with capital at Sennar. Funj Sultanate became most important Islamic state in Sudanese history, controlling vast areas of central and eastern Sudan. State based on agriculture and pastoralism, developing prosperous trade networks.

events.title: Islamic Scholarly Center
events.description: Sennar became important Islamic scholarly and religious center, attracting scholars from across Islamic world. Sufi orders spread widely in Sudan, profoundly influencing local Islamic practice. Quranic schools (khalwas) established throughout region, training religious scholars and judges. This period laid foundation for Sudan's Islamic culture.

events.title: Islamization Process
events.description: Under Funj Sultanate rule, Islam spread widely throughout Sudan. Sufi orders played important role, establishing religious schools and mosques. Arabic became official language and Islamic law was implemented. This period formed Sudan's unique Islamic culture, blending Arab, Nubian and African traditional elements.

events.title: Funj-Ottoman Relations
events.description: Funj Sultanate established diplomatic relations with Ottoman Empire, recognizing Ottoman Sultan's religious leadership. However Funj maintained political independence, with boundary maintained between Ottoman-controlled Egypt and Funj. This balanced relationship allowed Funj to develop independently while gaining connections with broader Islamic world. Trade routes linked Sudan, Egypt and Red Sea region.

events.title: Funj Sultanate Decline
events.description: Funj Sultanate's central authority gradually weakened, with local lords and Hamaj (military aristocracy) expanding autonomy. Royal internal conflicts frequent, succession crises continuous. By mid-18th century, actual power fell into hands of Hamaj prime minister. Economic decline, slave trade conflicts and external pressures intensified kingdom's instability. This created conditions for later Egyptian conquest.

events.title: Egyptian Conquest of Sudan
events.description: Egyptian Governor Muhammad Ali sent armies to conquer Sudan, establishing Egyptian-Sudanese regime. Conquering army used modern weapons, easily defeating Funj Sultanate and other local forces. Egyptian rule brought modernization reforms but also increased tax burden and forced conscription of slaves and soldiers.

events.title: Foundation of Khartoum
events.description: Egyptian rulers established city of Khartoum at confluence of Blue and White Niles as Sudan's administrative center. Khartoum rapidly developed into important trade and military outpost, connecting northern and southern Sudan. City became symbol of Egyptian rule in Sudan and origin of modern Sudan's capital.

events.title: Expansion of Sudanese Slave Trade
events.description: Egyptian rulers massively expanded Sudan's slave trade, mainly targeting southern non-Muslim regions. Thousands of slaves captured annually and transported to Egypt and Middle East. Slave trade became important revenue source for Egyptian-Sudanese regime, but caused population decline and social destruction in southern regions. This exploitation deepened north-south hatred, planting seeds for future conflicts.

events.title: Darfur Incorporated into Egyptian-Sudan
events.description: Egyptian army conquered Darfur region, incorporating it into Egyptian-Sudanese regime. Darfur had been independent Islamic sultanate with long history and culture. Conquest brought Egyptian administrative management and taxation system. Darfur's rich resources and strategic location made it important province in western Sudan.

events.title: Baker's Expedition and Equatoria Province
events.description: British explorer Samuel Baker commissioned by Egypt to explore upper White Nile region, establishing Equatoria Province. Baker attempted to eliminate slave trade in region but faced strong resistance from slave traders. This expedition expanded Egyptian-Sudanese regime's control over south, while introducing European influence in Sudanese affairs.

events.title: Gordon's Governorship
events.description: British officer Charles Gordon appointed as Governor-General of Sudan, implementing anti-slavery policies. Gordon attempted to modernize administrative management and establish more effective government. He dispatched expeditions deep into south, expanding Egyptian control. However anti-slavery policies harmed interests of many merchants and tribal chiefs, causing widespread discontent. Gordon's reforms planted seeds for later Mahdist uprising.

events.title: Mahdist Uprising Begins
events.description: Muhammad Ahmad declared himself Mahdi (savior), launching uprising in western Sudan against Egyptian-British rule. Mahdist movement combined religious fervor with nationalist sentiment, quickly gaining widespread support. Rebel forces used guerrilla tactics, repeatedly defeating government armies.

events.title: Mahdist State Rule
events.description: Khalifa Abdullah ruled Mahdist state for 13 years, implementing strict Islamic law. State faced economic difficulties, famine and external threats. Mahdist regime attempted to establish pure Islamic society but lacked effective administrative management. During this period Sudan was largely isolated from outside world, modernization process stagnated.

events.title: Fall of Khartoum
events.description: Mahdist forces captured Khartoum, killing British Governor General Gordon. This event shocked Britain and Europe, becoming major Victorian era incident. Mahdist state formally established, controlling most of Sudan. Mahdi himself died shortly after victory, succeeded by Khalifa Abdullah.

events.title: Battle of Omdurman
events.description: British-Egyptian forces under General Kitchener defeated Mahdist army at Omdurman. Modern weapons' huge advantage gave allied forces decisive victory, Khalifa Abdullah killed in battle. This battle marked end of Mahdist state and beginning of Anglo-Egyptian Sudan era.

events.title: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan Established
events.description: Britain and Egypt signed agreement establishing Anglo-Egyptian Sudan condominium. Though nominally joint rule, actual control was in British hands. British Governor-General ruled Sudan, implementing indirect rule policy. This system lasted over half century, profoundly affecting Sudan's political and social development.

events.title: Fashoda Incident Aftermath
events.description: After Fashoda Crisis resolution, Britain and France delineated spheres of influence in Sudan and West Africa. Britain consolidated control over Sudan, while France recognized British dominance in Nile basin. This diplomatic resolution avoided war between European powers, establishing colonial Africa's border patterns.

events.title: Aswan Dam Construction
events.description: Britain began constructing Aswan Dam in Egypt, significantly impacting Sudan's Nile water resource management. Dam controlled Nile water flow, affecting Sudan's agricultural irrigation. This marked beginning of modern hydraulic engineering transformation of Nile Basin, also planting seeds of future Sudan-Egypt water disputes.

events.title: Gordon Memorial College Established
events.description: Britain established Gordon Memorial College (later University of Khartoum) in Khartoum, Sudan's first modern higher education institution. College trained Sudanese administrators and technicians, using English as teaching language. This college became cradle of Sudan's modern intellectuals, with many future nationalist leaders educated there.

events.title: Final Conquest of Darfur Sultanate
events.description: British forces suppressed last resistance in Darfur region, with Sultan Ali Dinar defeated and killed. Darfur completely incorporated into Anglo-Egyptian Sudan. This marked Britain's establishment of rule throughout Sudan, with all local forces' independent resistance crushed. Darfur integrated into colonial administrative system.

events.title: North-South Separation Policy
events.description: Britain implemented 'Closed Districts Policy,' separating Christian and animist south from Islamized north administratively. Northern merchants and religious figures prohibited from entering south, with English rather than Arabic promoted in south. This policy deepened cultural, religious and economic divide between north and south, planting seeds for future division and civil war.

events.title: Assassination of Sir Lee Stack
events.description: British Commander-in-Chief of Egyptian Army Sir Lee Stack assassinated in Cairo, with Britain blaming Egyptian nationalists. Britain forced all Egyptian officers and officials to withdraw from Sudan, ending nominal condominium and effectively becoming sole British rule. This event reshaped Sudan's political landscape.

events.title: 1924 Revolution
events.description: Sudanese officers and intellectuals launched anti-British uprising, demanding independence and unity with Egypt. Though uprising was suppressed, it marked rise of Sudanese nationalist movement. British authorities expelled Egyptian officials, strengthening direct control over Sudan. This event deepened divisions between northern and southern Sudan.

events.title: Modern Economic Development Begins
events.description: Britain promoted modern economic development in Sudan, with Gezira Irrigation Scheme becoming one of world's largest cotton cultivation projects. Railways, ports and communication systems expanded. Cash crop exports increased, but traditional subsistence agriculture impacted. Economic modernization mainly concentrated in north, with south lagging behind and economic gap widening.

events.title: Graduates' Congress Formed
events.description: Sudan's educated elite formed Graduates' Congress, becoming first modern political organization. Congress demanded greater political participation and eventual independence. This marked beginning of Sudan's modern political movement, laying foundation for later independence struggle.

events.title: During World War II
events.description: Sudan served as Allied logistics base, supporting North African campaign. Tens of thousands of Sudanese soldiers served in British army, participating in East and North African battlefields. War economy stimulated Sudan's development but also caused material shortages and inflation. War experience heightened Sudanese political consciousness, with nationalist movement accelerating after war.

events.title: Sudan Administrative Council Established
events.description: British authorities established Sudan Administrative Council, allowing Sudanese participation in government administration. This was important step toward self-governance. Council comprised Sudanese and British officials, discussing Sudan's administrative and economic affairs. This reform laid institutional foundation for Sudanese independence.

events.title: Self-Government Agreement
events.description: Britain, Egypt and Sudan signed self-government agreement, granting Sudan internal autonomy. Agreement stipulated referendum after three years to decide independence or unity with Egypt. Sudan began preparing for independence, establishing own government institutions and army. Southern Sudan expressed concerns about these arrangements.

events.title: First Sudanese Civil War
events.description: Southern Sudan launched armed rebellion against northern Arab Muslim rule. War caused hundreds of thousands of deaths and massive refugee displacement. Conflict rooted in religious, cultural, economic and political differences. South demanded autonomy and equal development, while northern government tried to forcibly implement Arabization and Islamization policies.

events.title: Sudan Independence
events.description: Sudan declared independence, becoming first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence. Ismail al-Azhari became first Prime Minister. Independence celebrations held in Khartoum, marking end of colonial era. However, independent Sudan faced serious north-south divisions and political instability.

events.title: Abboud Military Coup
events.description: General Ibrahim Abboud launched military coup, overthrowing elected government and establishing military dictatorship. Abboud regime implemented harsh Arabization and Islamization policies, exacerbating north-south tensions. Coup set precedent for military rule in Sudan, with military coups becoming norm in Sudanese politics thereafter.

events.title: October Revolution
events.description: Students and workers launched massive demonstrations, overthrowing Abboud military government and restoring civilian rule. This revolution called 'October Revolution' demonstrated Sudanese people's desire for democracy. However, new government faced serious economic difficulties and continuing southern war, political situation remained unstable.

events.title: Nimeiry Coup
events.description: Colonel Jaafar Nimeiry launched military coup, establishing Revolutionary Command Council. Nimeiry initially adopted socialist policies, building close relations with Soviet Union. He implemented land reform and nationalization policies, attempting to solve Sudan's economic and social problems.

events.title: Addis Ababa Agreement
events.description: Sudanese government and Southern Sudan Liberation Movement signed Addis Ababa Agreement, ending first civil war. Agreement granted southern Sudan autonomy, recognizing its cultural and religious diversity. This brought ten years of peace, viewed as successful example of African conflict resolution.

events.title: Islamic Law Implementation and Second Civil War Begins
events.description: President Nimeiry declared implementation of Islamic law (Sharia), abolishing Addis Ababa Agreement. This decision triggered Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) armed uprising, beginning second Sudanese civil war. War was more devastating than first, lasting 22 years.

events.title: Fall of Nimeiry Regime
events.description: Popular uprising overthrew Nimeiry regime, establishing transitional military council. Economic crisis, famine and continuing war caused regime to lose popular support. New government promised democratic restoration but faced enormous challenges including economic collapse and southern war.

events.title: Bashir Military Coup
events.description: Brigadier Omar al-Bashir launched military coup, overthrowing elected government and establishing 'Revolutionary Command Council for National Salvation.' Bashir allied with Islamist Hassan al-Turabi, establishing Islamist regime. This marked beginning of 30 years of dictatorship in Sudan.

events.title: International Sanctions and Isolation
events.description: Due to supporting terrorism and human rights violations, Sudan faced international sanctions and isolation. US designated Sudan as state sponsor of terrorism, implementing comprehensive sanctions. Economic sanctions exacerbated Sudan's economic difficulties, but Bashir regime maintained Islamist policies.

events.title: Al-Shifa Factory Bombing
events.description: US bombed Al-Shifa pharmaceutical factory in Khartoum under anti-terrorism pretext, claiming factory produced chemical weapons. Sudan denied allegations, stating factory only produced medicines. This incident escalated US-Sudan tensions, becoming international controversy.

events.title: Turabi-Bashir Split
events.description: President Bashir and Islamist leader Turabi engaged in power struggle, with Bashir ultimately victorious. Bashir dissolved parliament, arrested Turabi, consolidating personal power. This marked major change in Sudan's political landscape, with Bashir beginning to monopolize power.

events.title: Oil Production Begins
events.description: Sudan began large-scale oil production, mainly involving Chinese, Malaysian and Indian companies. Oil revenues provided important funding source for government but also intensified north-south conflict as most oil fields located in south. Oil became important factor in civil war.

events.title: Darfur Crisis Erupts
events.description: Armed conflict erupted in western Sudan's Darfur region, with government-backed Arab militia 'Janjaweed' conducting ethnic cleansing against African tribes. UN called this genocide, causing hundreds of thousands of deaths and millions of refugees. Darfur crisis became international focus.

events.title: Darfur Humanitarian Crisis
events.description: Darfur conflict escalated into severe humanitarian crisis, with UN and international organizations intervening to provide humanitarian aid. Janjaweed militia conducted systematic attacks on African tribal villages, causing massive civilian casualties. International Criminal Court began investigating war crimes by Sudanese government and militia. This crisis attracted global attention.

events.title: Comprehensive Peace Agreement
events.description: Sudanese government and Sudan People's Liberation Army signed Comprehensive Peace Agreement (CPA), ending 22-year civil war. Agreement granted southern Sudan autonomy with independence referendum after six years. John Garang became Sudan's First Vice President but died in plane crash three weeks later.

events.title: Bashir Wanted by International Criminal Court
events.description: International Criminal Court issued arrest warrant for President Bashir, charging him with war crimes and crimes against humanity in Darfur. This was ICC's first arrest warrant for sitting head of state. Bashir refused to recognize court's jurisdiction, continuing in power.

events.title: South Sudan Independence
events.description: Following referendum, South Sudan declared independence, becoming world's youngest nation. Independence celebrations held in Juba with Salva Kiir as first president. Sudan lost three-quarters of oil resources and quarter of territory, facing serious economic crisis.

events.title: Anti-Government Protests Begin
events.description: Due to economic crisis and bread price increases, Sudan erupted in large-scale anti-government protests. Demonstrations initially began in Atbara, quickly spreading nationwide. Protesters demanded Bashir's resignation, ending 30 years of dictatorship.

events.title: Protest Movement Escalates
events.description: Protest movement continued escalating, spreading nationwide. Sudanese Professionals Association led protest activities, demanding regime change. Government intensified crackdown, but protesters persisted with nonviolent resistance. Signs of division appeared within military, with some officers expressing sympathy for protesters. International community closely monitored situation developments.

events.title: Bashir Overthrown by Military
events.description: After four months of protests, Sudanese military launched coup, overthrowing President Bashir. Transitional Military Council took power, promising democratic transition. Bashir was arrested, ending 30 years of rule. This event called 'Sudanese Revolution.'

events.title: Sovereign Council Formed
events.description: Military and civilian opposition reached agreement, forming Sovereign Council as transitional government. Council jointly composed of military and civilians, with Abdel Fattah al-Burhan as chairman. Agreement stipulated 39-month transition period, ultimately holding democratic elections.

events.title: Military Coup
events.description: General Burhan launched military coup, dissolving transitional government and arresting civilian leaders. Coup triggered international condemnation and sanctions, with Sudanese people taking to streets in protest again. This marked interruption of democratic transition process, Sudan falling into political crisis again.

events.title: Armed Conflict Erupts
events.description: Intense armed conflict erupted between Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces, fighting spreading to major cities including Khartoum. Conflict caused thousands of deaths and millions of displaced persons. International community called for ceasefire, but negotiation efforts repeatedly failed.

events.title: Humanitarian Crisis
events.description: Ongoing armed conflict led Sudan to face severe humanitarian crisis. Over 10 million people need humanitarian assistance, millions face famine threat. International aid affected by security situation, difficult to reach people needing help. Sudan's economy completely collapsed, infrastructure severely damaged. UN warned this could become one of world's largest humanitarian disasters.

events.title: Famine Warning
events.description: UN and humanitarian organizations warned Sudan faces massive famine risk, particularly in Darfur and Kordofan regions. Armed conflict obstructs humanitarian aid delivery, agricultural production collapsed. Millions of children face severe malnutrition. International community increased aid efforts, but security situation makes relief work extremely difficult.
